title: Fentanyl-induced postural changes across species: behaviors, mechanisms, and translational implications
abstract: This narrative review summarizes fentanyl-induced postural effects across species, focusing on a postulated cerulospinal noradrenergic connection linking rodent catalepsy models to human wooden-chest syndrome (WCS). This could have possible translational relevance for fentanyl overdose and its clinical management. A review of English-language literature was conducted using PubMed and EMBASE. Reference lists of retrieved articles and prior reviews on the topic were searched for additional sources. The evidence supports that fentanyl-induced postural effects are centrally mediated to a significant extent through µ-opioid receptor (MOR) activation in the locus cœruleus, with downstream engagement of cerulospinal noradrenergic projections onto spinal α 1 -adrenoceptors. Further, this integrated pathway is subject to modulation by nitric oxide and glutamatergic signaling, striatal dopaminergic–medium spiny neuron circuitry, and pontine respiratory nuclei. Phenomenology differs substantially across species, dose, and route of administration, but a phylogenetically conserved MOR–cerulospinal–noradrenergic pathway, modulated by nitric oxide and dopaminergic circuitry, appears to underlie fentanyl-induced postural disturbances across species, from cataleptic immobility in rodents to WCS in humans. The conserved mechanism is expressed as species-specific chest-wall mechanics that are a determinant of clinical severity, and helps to understand the potential role of α 2 -adrenoceptor agonists as being mechanistically rational for overdose management.
